topic: Hazards and uses of radioactive emissions and of background radiation (physics only)
subject: physics

items.q: Which statement about background radiation is correct?
items.correct: It is around us all of the time, from natural and man-made sources.
items.misconception: It is only present in places affected by a nuclear accident.
items.why: Radiation is almost only mentioned in the news in connection with accidents and weapons, so students associate its presence with disaster rather than with everyday life. Background radiation is present continuously and everywhere. It comes from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space, as well as from man-made sources. An accident can raise the level in a place, but it does not create radiation where there was none before.
items.random_wrong: It exists only because humans have used nuclear technology.

items.q: Which of these sources of background radiation is a natural source?
items.correct: Cosmic rays arriving from outer space
items.misconception: Fallout left by nuclear weapons testing
items.why: Students classify by what a substance is made of rather than by how it came to be there, and they know uranium is a naturally occurring element. The classification is by origin. Rocks and cosmic rays from space were there without human action, so they are natural. Fallout is spread across the Earth because people tested weapons or because a reactor failed, so it is man-made.
items.random_wrong: Emissions released in a nuclear accident

items.q: People who live high up a mountain receive a larger radiation dose from cosmic rays than people at sea level. Why?
items.correct: There is less atmosphere above them to absorb the cosmic rays.
items.misconception: They are further from the radioactive rocks in the ground.
items.why: Students correctly learn that radiation gets weaker with distance from a source, then apply that idea to the ground while forgetting the second natural source named in the specification. There is a source above as well as below. Cosmic rays come from space and are absorbed by the atmosphere, so at high altitude, with less atmosphere overhead, more of them reach you and the dose from them is higher.
items.random_wrong: Cosmic rays are produced by the thinner air found high up.

items.q: Which pair are both man-made sources of background radiation?
items.correct: Fallout from weapons testing and nuclear accidents
items.misconception: Fallout from weapons testing and cosmic rays
items.why: The Sun is the only object in space students routinely link with radiation reaching the Earth, so 'from space' is read as 'from the Sun'. Cosmic rays arrive from space in general, not only from the Sun, and background radiation is present continuously. Their contribution to dose depends on where you are — for example it is greater at high altitude — not on the time of day.
items.random_wrong: Rocks in the ground and fallout from nuclear accidents

items.q: A radiographer wears a badge at work that records the radiation dose she receives, and her total dose each year is checked. Which statement best explains why this is done?
items.correct: Her occupation can raise the radiation dose she receives.
items.misconception: Everyone receives the same dose, so all workers are checked.
items.why: The word 'background' suggests a constant baseline, and textbook questions often quote a single average value for a country as if it applied to every person in it. A quoted background figure is an average. A person living where the rock contains more radioactive isotopes, or at high altitude, or working with radioactive sources, receives a different dose from the average.
items.random_wrong: The badge lowers the dose the radiographer receives at work.

items.q: Two identical houses are built in different parts of the country, one on granite and one on clay. Which statement about the background radiation in the two houses is correct?
items.correct: Background level can differ because the rocks differ.
items.misconception: Both houses have exactly the same background level.
items.why: The word 'background' suggests a constant baseline, and textbook questions often quote a single average value for a country as if it applied to every person in it. A quoted background figure is an average. A person living where the rock contains more radioactive isotopes, or at high altitude, or working with radioactive sources, receives a different dose from the average.
items.random_wrong: The clay house has more because clay is denser rock.

items.q: A worker's radiation dose for one year is recorded as 3.6 millisieverts (mSv). What does this dose tell you?
items.correct: The risk of harm from the radiation received.
items.misconception: The number of decays each second in the source.
items.why: Both quantities are met in the same topic and both get bigger when there is 'more radiation', so students merge them into a single idea of strength. Activity is a property of the source: decays per second, in becquerels. Dose is a property of the person exposed: the risk of harm from the radiation their body received, in sieverts. The same source gives different doses to people standing at different distances.
items.random_wrong: The energy stored in the radioactive source used.

items.q: A patient receives a radiation dose of 4.5 mSv. Given that 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?
items.why: Students recall that centimetres and metres differ by 100 and transfer that factor to any prefix conversion instead of using the relationship given. Use the relationship as it is stated: 1000 mSv = 1 sievert. So a dose in mSv is divided by 1000 to give sieverts, and a dose in Sv is multiplied by 1000 to give millisieverts.

items.q: In one year worker P receives a dose of 0.8 mSv and worker Q receives a dose of 0.0015 Sv. Use 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). Which comparison is correct?
items.correct: Q receives the higher dose, about twice that of P.
items.misconception: P receives the higher dose, as 0.8 is the larger number.
items.why: Students recall that centimetres and metres differ by 100 and transfer that factor to any prefix conversion instead of using the relationship given. Use the relationship as it is stated: 1000 mSv = 1 sievert. So a dose in mSv is divided by 1000 to give sieverts, and a dose in Sv is multiplied by 1000 to give millisieverts.
items.random_wrong: The two doses are equal once the units are converted.

items.q: Which statement about the half-lives of radioactive isotopes is correct?
items.correct: They range from fractions of a second to billions of years.
items.misconception: They are all of a similar length, around a few years.
items.why: Practice questions use convenient values such as 2 days or 5 years, so students never meet the extremes and assume the range is narrow. Half-lives range from tiny fractions of a second to thousands of millions of years. That range is exactly why the hazard from different radioactive materials differs so much.
items.random_wrong: The most hazardous isotopes always have the longest ones.

items.q: Two sealed sources contain the same number of undecayed nuclei. Source X has a half-life of 8 days and source Y has a half-life of 1600 years. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: X gives the higher activity now, but for a shorter time.
items.misconception: Y is more hazardous now because its half-life is longer.
items.why: 'Long' is read as 'more', and students know a long-lived waste isotope is described as dangerous, so they conclude that long half-life equals high activity. Half-life is the time for the activity, or the number of undecayed nuclei, to halve. A long half-life means the nuclei decay slowly, so the activity is lower now — but the material stays radioactive for a very long time, which is a different kind of hazard.
items.random_wrong: X is completely harmless because it decays away fast.

items.q: Radioactive material is spilled on a laboratory floor. Why is a spill of an isotope with a half-life of 30 years a longer-term problem than a spill of one with a half-life of 6 hours?
items.correct: It stays significantly radioactive for many decades.
items.misconception: The 30-year isotope emits far more radiation each second.
items.why: 'Long' is read as 'more', and students know a long-lived waste isotope is described as dangerous, so they conclude that long half-life equals high activity. Half-life is the time for the activity, or the number of undecayed nuclei, to halve. A long half-life means the nuclei decay slowly, so the activity is lower now — but the material stays radioactive for a very long time, which is a different kind of hazard.
items.random_wrong: A spill of the 6-hour isotope emits no radiation at all.

items.q: A patient is given a small amount of a radioactive substance so that doctors can follow where it goes inside the body. This is an example of:
items.correct: exploring internal organs with nuclear radiation
items.misconception: destroying unwanted tissue with nuclear radiation
items.why: Diagrams show a single arrow ending at the tumour, which suggests the radiation stops there rather than passing through tissue on the way in and out. Radiation reaching the tumour has to pass through healthy tissue, and some of that tissue is damaged. Treatment is planned to keep this as small as possible — for example by directing beams at the tumour from several different directions so the tumour receives a high dose while each path through healthy tissue receives much less — but the risk is reduced, not removed.
items.random_wrong: reducing the patient's background radiation dose

items.q: Which combination of properties makes an isotope suitable for use as a medical tracer?
items.correct: It emits gamma radiation and has a short half-life.
items.misconception: It emits alpha radiation, which is strongly ionising.
items.why: Students carry over 'strongly ionising means a strong effect' from the hazard topic without asking what has to happen for a tracer to work at all. A tracer has to be detected outside the body, so its radiation must be penetrating enough to get out — gamma radiation. Being strongly ionising is a drawback here, not an advantage: alpha radiation absorbed by the patient's tissue delivers dose without producing any image.
items.random_wrong: It has a very long half-life so it lasts in storage.

items.q: During radiotherapy, gamma radiation is aimed at a tumour from several different directions. Which statement best explains why?
items.correct: The tumour gets a high dose while healthy tissue gets less.
items.misconception: Healthy tissue is not affected by gamma radiation at all.
items.why: Diagrams show a single arrow ending at the tumour, which suggests the radiation stops there rather than passing through tissue on the way in and out. Radiation reaching the tumour has to pass through healthy tissue, and some of that tissue is damaged. Treatment is planned to keep this as small as possible — for example by directing beams at the tumour from several different directions so the tumour receives a high dose while each path through healthy tissue receives much less — but the risk is reduced, not removed.
items.random_wrong: Gamma radiation only damages cells where beams overlap.

items.q: A doctor must decide whether to use a radioactive tracer scan on a patient. Which approach is the best way to evaluate this use of nuclear radiation?
items.correct: Weigh the dose received against the benefit of a diagnosis.
items.misconception: Refuse it, because every use of radiation carries a risk.
items.why: The hazards of radiation are taught vividly and separately from the benefits, and public feeling about radiation is stronger than about most other medical risks. An evaluation compares both sides using the figures given. A scan dose that is a fraction of the dose received from background radiation in a year may allow a disease to be found and treated, and an untreated tumour may be far more likely to kill the patient than the treatment is to harm them.
items.random_wrong: Accept it, because medical scans are always safe for patients.

items.q: A hospital leaflet states that a chest scan gives a dose of about 0.1 mSv, and that the average dose from background radiation in the UK is about 2.7 mSv per year. Which conclusion do these data best support?
items.correct: The scan adds much less than a year of background dose.
items.misconception: The scan should be refused because any dose is harmful.
items.why: The hazards of radiation are taught vividly and separately from the benefits, and public feeling about radiation is stronger than about most other medical risks. An evaluation compares both sides using the figures given. A scan dose that is a fraction of the dose received from background radiation in a year may allow a disease to be found and treated, and an untreated tumour may be far more likely to kill the patient than the treatment is to harm them.
items.random_wrong: Background dose is the same for everyone, so this is exact.

items.q: Radiotherapy to destroy a tumour also carries a risk of damaging healthy cells. Which statement is the best evaluation of that risk?
items.correct: The risk is smaller than that of leaving the cancer.
items.misconception: Radiotherapy should never be offered to any patient.
items.why: The hazards of radiation are taught vividly and separately from the benefits, and public feeling about radiation is stronger than about most other medical risks. An evaluation compares both sides using the figures given. A scan dose that is a fraction of the dose received from background radiation in a year may allow a disease to be found and treated, and an untreated tumour may be far more likely to kill the patient than the treatment is to harm them.
items.random_wrong: There is no risk, since beams reach only the tumour.

items.q: Are the ordinary rocks under a house a source of background radiation?
items.correct: Yes. Rocks are given by the specification as an example of a natural source.
items.misconception: Ordinary rocks are not radioactive — only uranium ore in a mine is.
items.why: Students meet radioactivity as something special and rare, kept in a lead box in a laboratory, so they do not expect the ground itself to be a source. Rocks contain small amounts of radioactive isotopes, so they emit radiation continuously. How much depends on the rock type, which is one reason the background level varies from place to place.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Would there still be background radiation if no one had ever built a reactor or tested a weapon?
items.correct: Yes. Natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space would still be there.
items.misconception: Background radiation exists because of nuclear technology — it is all left over from power stations and bombs.
items.why: The man-made sources are the ones students hear about, so they assume those sources account for the whole of the background. Background radiation has two kinds of source. The natural ones — rocks and cosmic rays from space — have always been present. Man-made sources such as the fallout from weapons testing and nuclear accidents add to that background; they are not the whole of it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: An isotope has a half-life of a few minutes. Does that mean it is harmless?
items.correct: No. A very short half-life means a very high activity while it lasts.
items.misconception: Something with a short half-life decays away almost at once, so it cannot do any harm.
items.why: Students focus on how long the hazard lasts and ignore how intense it is, because half-life is taught as a time rather than as a rate of decay. A short half-life means a large number of decays each second, so the radiation emitted is intense and the hazard while it lasts is severe. What is true is that the hazard does not persist: the activity falls quickly, which is why short half-life isotopes are chosen for use inside the body.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: After a tracer scan, is the patient radioactive for the rest of their life?
items.correct: No. A tracer isotope is chosen so that its activity falls quickly after the scan.
items.misconception: Once you have been given a radioactive substance you stay radioactive permanently.
items.why: Students think of contamination as something that soaks in and stays, and they do not connect the choice of isotope with how long the activity lasts. The isotope used has a half-life long enough for the scan to be completed but short enough that the activity falls away rapidly afterwards, so the dose the patient receives is limited.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A patient's dose is given as 0.5 mSv. Is that the mass of radioactive material they took in?
items.correct: No. Radiation dose measures the risk of harm from the radiation the body received.
items.misconception: Dose is like a dose of medicine — it is the amount of radioactive substance given to the person.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'dose' is a quantity of a substance, so students read the word as an amount of material rather than as an effect on the body. Radiation dose is not an amount of substance. It is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from the body being exposed to ionising radiation, and it is measured in sieverts. A person standing near a source receives a dose without any material entering them at all.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: To change a dose of 3 mSv into sieverts, do you multiply by 1000?
items.correct: No. You divide by 1000, giving 0.003 Sv.
items.misconception: Converting units always means multiplying by the number in the relationship.
items.why: Students see '1000' in the relationship and reach for multiplication without checking whether the answer should come out larger or smaller. 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, so a millisievert is the smaller unit. A dose expressed in the smaller unit gives a smaller number in sieverts, so divide by 1000. Check the answer is smaller than the number you started with.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the half-life of a spilled radioactive material affect how long the area stays a hazard?
items.correct: Yes. The longer the half-life, the longer the material stays significantly radioactive.
items.misconception: Half-life is just a number used in decay calculations; how dangerous a spill is depends only on how much was spilled.
items.why: Half-life is usually met in graph and calculation questions, so students treat it as a piece of arithmetic rather than as the thing that decides how long a hazard lasts. Half-life sets both how intense the emission is now and how long the material remains a problem. A spill with a half-life of hours becomes safe within days; one with a half-life of tens of years contaminates the area for a human lifetime.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
